Slide 44: How many of you have heard LLM's are just statistical models that suck up tons of data and based on all that data they predict what word will come next?
Slide 45: It is true the output of an LLM is a next word prediction, but I think to just call the LLM a statistical model, does a disservice, and leads to misconceptions

Slide 48: Moreover, why are there so many different variants of the same open source model? We can see Meta put out dozens of Llama variants
Slide 49: An LLM will typically go through multiple alignment steps after the initial data training, and typically the safety alignment is done at the very end.

Slide 50: We find a huge difference in the abilities of these variants, in what they call their base model, we ask it how to make a sandwich and it tells us that Newark is the capital of NJ. Which is a true fact. But not what we asked.
Slide 51: In a different variant that meta fine tuned to behave more like a chatbot, we actually get our sandwich instructions.

Slide 52: And in a 3rd variant, one that's designed to think, we get a lot of introspection and insights about sandwich building before we get our steps. What's kind of crazy about thinking models is the output is evaluated against a reward function using a simple reinforcement learning technique, but the thinking step isn't evaluated as part of the reward function. Which means the models sort of teach themselves what and how to think.

Slide 53: This of course begs the question, can the safety step be easily unlearned with the same methods? And the answer shouldn't surprise you, that yes you can do this.
